title: The Deal Washington Lost: How The Hill and Tehran Times Agreed
subtitle: A US centrist policy outlet and Iran's state-aligned press independently reached the same conclusion about who won the Hormuz negotiation.
body_md:
Iran and Oman announced on August 5–6, 2026 that they had agreed on geographic coordinates for a new Strait of Hormuz shipping corridor and were finalising a joint statement. Even as the announcement circulated, an oil tanker passing through the strait reported hearing two explosions. Hundreds of vessels remained stranded. [AFP / France 24 EN](https://www.france24.com/en/middle-east/20260806-middle-east-live-israeli-military-says-two-soldiers-killed-in-southern-lebanon) The diplomatic and the kinetic were running in parallel, as they have throughout the five months since the US-Israeli strikes that launched this conflict.

The Hill, a centrist US policy outlet, assessed the emerging deal as "the biggest concession yet given to Tehran in its control of the Strait of Hormuz." [The Hill](https://thehill.com/) Tehran Times, Iran's state-aligned English-language press, concluded that "the United States has increasingly pinned its hopes on negotiations between Tehran and Muscat" after "dwindling strategic resources" — a position framing Washington as the party under pressure. [Tehran Times](https://www.tehrantimes.com/news/528884/Iran-Oman-move-to-finalize-new-Hormuz-shipping-corridor) Two outlets from opposite sides of the conflict independently reached the same conclusion: the bilateral Iran-Oman channel has sidelined Washington, and the deal's terms represent a strategic gain for Tehran. That convergence is the single clearest signal in 87 articles across 22 countries.

The shared frame for most of the corpus was diplomatic progress, oil-price relief, and economic consequence. LaBSE cosine similarity between India and wire services reached 0.936 — the highest pairing in this corpus — and UK and Southeast Asian coverage reached 0.934. [Globe and Mail](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/world/article-us-iran-strait-of-hormuz/) The Globe and Mail captured the scale: the strait was once the passage for a fifth of the world's traded oil and natural gas; its closure has driven up fuel and basic goods globally. Tehran Times supplied the commodity-shock figures, citing UN/ITC data: LNG exports from affected economies down 95 percent, urea exports down 83 percent, Japan's crude oil imports down 64 percent.

The most isolated buckets in this corpus — pan-Arab (mean LaBSE similarity 0.607) and pan-African (0.652) — reflect fundamentally different editorial angles. Middle East Eye foregrounded the maritime security incident: two blasts, a region still at war. AfricaNews foregrounded the humanitarian shipping impact: hundreds of vessels stranded, livelihoods disrupted. Both angles are real; neither is what most wire-service coverage led with.

The deal's structural fragility barely registered in mainstream coverage. Hindustan Times was the only outlet to detail that three competing versions of key terms circulate simultaneously: the Wall Street Journal reported the draft would give Tehran oversight without fees; Reuters reported Iran was seeking 5–7 percent cargo fees; IRNA stated that fee collection would depend on decisions by Iran's "highest authorities" and on US conduct. [BBC World](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckg9d3eyeggo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss) More critically, Hindustan Times alone reported that the IRGC — which physically enforces maritime restrictions — is not at the negotiating table. A deal that Iran's military arm has not endorsed is not yet a deal. The Globe and Mail added the capstone: the agreement awaits Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei's approval, and Khamenei "is believed to have been wounded in the war's opening strikes and has not been seen in public since."

Japan and Saudi Arabia are absent from this corpus. Japan's crude oil imports have fallen 64 percent due to Hormuz disruption — the largest supply impact on any US ally — yet no Japanese outlet covered the Iran-Oman talks; Japanese press likely focused on domestic energy contingency. Saudi Arabia was simultaneously being struck: Houthis hit the 8th and 9th Saudi oil tankers since launching a Saudi blockade, a direct national security story that Saudi state media apparently treated as separate from the Hormuz diplomacy. The two most directly affected non-Iranian countries both looked away.

Trump said on August 6 that the Strait of Hormuz was "gonna be open very soon, or Iran is gonna get hit." [Haaretz](https://www.haaretz.com/middle-east-news/iran/2026-08-05/ty-article/trump-hormuz-strait-gonna-be-open-very-soon-or-iran-is-gonna-get-hit/0000019f-d06a-d147-adff-f17f2d820000) Iran's foreign ministry denied any direct negotiations with the US; ANSA Italian reported Tehran's position directly: "We're not negotiating with the US on Hormuz — only with Oman." [ANSA Italian (Mondo)](https://www.ansa.it/sito/notizie/mondo/mediooriente/2026/08/06/iran-non-stiamo-negoziando-con-gli-usa-su-hormuz-solo-con_077dcc2e-3125-4cb4-a508-acc3a89804e6.html) Haaretz's Israel-specific angle — the only outlet to connect Trump's threat to the US missile stockpile depletion as a constraint on military options — adds the layer that the coercion framing depends on resources Trump may not have.

The question of whether the deal that eventually emerges is the one the US said it would never accept — cementing Iran's grip over the strait — remains unresolved by this corpus. What the corpus has resolved is that two outlets with opposite institutional interests have already decided the answer.
